newsitem.title: USA: Cartoonist Lurie wants to sue Egyptian magazine.
newsitem.headline: Cartoonist Lurie wants to sue Egyptian magazine.

text.p: An Israeli-American cartoonist whose work has been barred in Egypt says he cannot find a lawyer to bring a libel suit against an Egyptian magazine that charges he was "a murderer" who took part in massacres of Egyptian soldiers.

Ranan Lurie, the world's most widely syndicated cartoonist, told Reuters on Friday he wants to sue Rose al-Youssef magazine for making what he said were competely false charges, but he said Egyptian lawyers are apparently not allowed to represent Israeli clients.

"I want to sue Rose al-Youssef for between $50 million and $80 million but I have to go through an Egyptian lawyer and they can't work for an Israeli. As a dual citizen of Israel and the United States I am now looking into suing as an American," he said.

The Egyptian daily Al Ahram stopped using Lurie's cartoons 11 days ago after a campaign launched by the magazine. Al Ahram said the suspension, only a month after it began using Lurie's work, would continue while it investigated the charges.

Lurie was the first Israeli to be syndicated in an Egyptian daily. Even though he has interviewed Egyptian President Hosni Murbarak twice and had a widely publicised TV interview with the late Anwar Sadat in 1977, the paper's decision to run his work was widely criticised.
Several Egyptian cartoonists said the paper's decision to run Lurie's work violated a ban on news organisations joining in the normalisation of relations with Israel.

Rose al-Youssef accused Lurie, who served as an Israeli army major in the 1967 Middle East war, of killing Egyptians in the Sinai. It also said he killed Algerians while with the French Foreign Legion.

Lurie said he never fought against Egyptians, never went to the Sinai as a soldier, never was in the French Foreign Legion and never set foot in Algeria. "In the 1967 war I was in the trenches facing Jordan and the Arab League," he said.
He said he was surprised by the campaign against him and bothered by cartoons of him in the Egyptian press that he regarded as anti-Semitic.

"I was always very well treated in Egypt. I was there last month and there was a party in my honour at the Nile Hilton attended by half the Egyptian cabinet and the foreign minister," he said. "I also had a 90-minute interview with President Murbarak in February and he complimented my efforts to show objectivity about the Middle East."
